| [LIT-308](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-308.md) v2 | Stochastic Thermodynamics of Learning | Goldt & Seifert (2017), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.010601. For a perceptron whose weights follow overdamped Langevin dynamics and whose predicted labels are fast two-state processes, the information learnt about fixed random labels is bounded by the weights' total entropy production: Σ_μ I(σ_T^μ:σ^μ) ≤ Σ_n [ΔS(ω_n) + ΔQ_n] (Eq. 16, k_B = T = 1). This defines a learning efficiency η ≤ 1. The cost side includes the change in the weights' own Shannon entropy, and in the paper's toy model η → 0.99 as the heat ΔQ → 0 (slow driving). | [LIT-327](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-327.md) v2 | Thermodynamics of Prediction | Still et al. (2012), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevLett.109.120604. | [LIT-360](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-360.md) v2 | Notes on Landauer's principle, reversible computation, and Maxwell's Demon | Bennett (2002), arXiv:physics/0210005. Bennett states Landauer's principle as a consequence of the Second Law. A logically irreversible step, meaning erasure or a *merge of control flow*, must export at least the lost entropy (k ln 2 per bit) to non-information-bearing degrees of freedom. That export need not take the form of heat (p. 1). Logically reversible operations, including copying onto a blank register and measurement, have no minimum cost. He calls "an intrinsic cost of order kT for every elementary act of information processing" a 20th-century "misconception" (pp. 5–6). Erasing random data can itself be thermodynamically reversible; the waste comes from applying a many-to-one operation to *known* data (pp. 1, 4). | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-310](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-310.md)); Worth reading as a short, first-hand statement, by the principle's main defender, of what Landauer's principle requires (logical irreversibility) and what it does not (any cost for acquiring, copying or evaluating information). On the Earman–Norton "unnecessary or insufficient" dilemma Bennett concedes the point "with some justice" (p. 5) and defends the principle only as pedagogy. |
| [LIT-515](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-515.md) | Statistical physics of self-replication | England (2012; J. Chem. Phys. 2013), arXiv:1209.1179. For a system in a heat bath obeying detailed balance, a transition between coarse-grained ensembles I → II obeys β⟨ΔQ⟩ + ln π(II→I) + ΔS_int ≥ 0 (Eq. 6), a second law stated for macrostates. Chem. Phys. text was not reached. Worth reading as the founding paper of the "dissipation-driven" programme and as a clean worked use of a macrostate fluctuation relation: the heat a replicator must release is bounded below by how fast it copies and how durable the copy is, not by the copying itself. The general bound (Eq. 6) is a coarse-grained second law and is sound; the numbers for E. coli and RNA rest on an argued, not derived, upper bound on the reverse probability (Eq. 7). | [LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md) | Time, Structure and Fluctuations | Prigogine (1977), Nobel Lecture, reprinted in Science 201:777 (1978). Near equilibrium the second-order excess entropy δ²S is a Lyapounov function, so fluctuations die out, and in the "strictly" linear regime the steady state minimizes entropy production. Far from equilibrium the sign of the excess entropy production ΣδJδX is no longer fixed. Given autocatalytic steps (necessary, not sufficient) the thermodynamic branch can go unstable, and fluctuations are amplified into "dissipative structures": Bénard convection, the Brusselator's limit cycle and "Turing bifurcation". A closing programme derives irreversibility from a non-unitary transformation of the Liouville dynamics. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-424](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-424.md)); worth reading as Prigogine's own short statement of the dissipative-structure programme, and as the place where its scope limits are stated in his words. A dissipative structure is a state beyond an instability of the "thermodynamic branch", "a giant fluctuation stabilized by exchanges of energy with the outside world". The minimum-entropy-production theorem is valid only in the "strictly" linear regime with constant phenomenological coefficients. Far from equilibrium the only general criterion offered is a sufficient one for stability (non-negative excess entropy production). Its §§6–7 programme of a non-unitary "entropy operator" is a sketch whose demonstrated link to macroscopic thermodynamics is, by its own account, "at least in the linear region". |
| [LIT-517](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-517.md) | Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences | Jarzynski (1997), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690. For a classical system that starts in canonical equilibrium and is switched from Hamiltonian H_0 to H_1 at any finite rate, the average of e^{−βW} over repetitions equals e^{−βΔF} (Eq. 2), whatever the path and the switching time. The proof is exact for an isolated system and for Nosé–Hoover thermostats, and needs weak coupling for a physical reservoir. Thermodynamic integration and the Zwanzig perturbation formula are its slow and fast limits, and ⟨W⟩ ≥ ΔF follows by Jensen. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-417](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-417.md)); worth reading as the four-page origin of the nonequilibrium work relation ⟨e^{−βW}⟩ = e^{−βΔF}: an equality, independent of path and switching rate, that turns irreversible work measurements into an equilibrium free-energy difference and gives ⟨W⟩ ≥ ΔF as a corollary by Jensen. | [LIT-518](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-518.md) | Statistical Physics of Adaptation | Perunov, Marsland & England (2014; Phys. Rev. X 2016), arXiv:1412.1875. Starting from a fluctuation relation between coarse-grained macrostates, the paper writes the log-odds of two outcomes of a driven system as an internal-entropy term, a reversal-probability term and Ψ − Φ, the mean heat minus a fluctuation correction (Eq. 8). Holding the first two fixed, the more likely outcome is the one whose formation absorbed and dissipated work from the drive more reliably. | [LIT-521](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-521.md) | Information theory explanation of the fluctuation theorem, maximum entropy production and self-organized criticality in non-equilibrium stationary states | Dewar (2003), DOI-10.1088/0305-4470/36/3/303. It applies Jaynes's maximum-entropy inference to the microscopic paths of an open system in a stationary state. Under fixed initial densities and boundary fluxes plus local conservation, the path distribution is p_Γ ∝ exp(A_Γ), with A_Γ carrying τσ_Γ/2k_B (Eq. 14). A fluctuation theorem and ⟨σ⟩ ≥ 0 follow (Eqs. 18–21). Then, in a mean-field approximation and assuming the number of paths increases with irreversible action, maximizing path entropy over the remaining multipliers is maximizing mean entropy production (MaxEP, Eq. 24). Read it as a programme, not a proof. The path distribution p_Γ ∝ exp(A_Γ) and its fluctuation theorem follow from the stated constraints. The MaxEP step needs a mean-field approximation and an assumption that the number of paths grows with their irreversible action, which is stated, not argued. | [LIT-522](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-522.md) | Entropy production fluctuation theorem and the nonequilibrium work relation for free energy differences | Crooks (1999), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevE.60.2721. For finite classical systems with stochastic, Markovian, microscopically reversible dynamics, the entropy production ω of a forward process and of its time reverse satisfy P_F(+ω)/P_R(−ω) = e^{ω} for any finite time, provided ω is odd under reversal. That holds for processes that start and end in equilibrium, where ω = β(W − ΔF), and for time-symmetric nonequilibrium steady states. The Jarzynski equality follows in one line, and for long times the theorem gives a heat fluctuation theorem and a Gaussian with variance twice the mean. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-413](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-413.md)); worth reading as the short paper that turned the entropy-production fluctuation theorem into a finite-time, trajectory-level statement for stochastic, microscopically reversible dynamics, P_F(+ω)/P_R(−ω) = e^{ω}, and derived the Jarzynski equality from it in a line. It also defines the trajectory entropy production ω = ln ρ(x_{−τ}) − ln ρ(x_{+τ}) − βQ that the record's stochastic-thermodynamics papers inherit. Read it knowing that its conditions are stated exactly (finite classical system, constant-intensive-parameter baths, Markovian microscopically reversible dynamics, ω odd under time reversal), and that the steady-state version is formally exact but, by the author's own account, of little practical use. |
| [LIT-523](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-523.md) | Stochastic thermodynamics, fluctuation theorems and molecular machines | Seifert (2012), DOI-10.1088/0034-4885/75/12/126001. A 105-page review of stochastic thermodynamics. Further results: dissipation bounds forward–reverse distinguishability (⟨w⟩ − ΔF ≥ D[p‖p_eq]), Sagawa–Ueda feedback relations, a NESS fluctuation–dissipation theorem in terms of entropy production, and a cycle-based theory of efficiency at maximum power for molecular machines. | Active — read 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-420](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-420.md); §§5, 8.3–8.4, 9.2 and 11 skimmed); worth reading as the systematic reference for stochastic thermodynamics as of 2012: first law, heat and stochastic entropy along single trajectories of Markovian systems coupled to baths, every known fluctuation theorem derived from one master theorem with a conjugate dynamics, dissipation as distinguishability of forward and reverse paths, Sagawa–Ueda feedback, the NESS fluctuation–dissipation theorem and efficiency of molecular machines. It is the framework in which the record's thermodynamics-of-prediction and thermodynamics-of-learning results ([LIT-327](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-327.md), [LIT-308](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-308.md)) are stated. Per its abstract: in a bistable system the kinetics of transitions between the two locally stable states can be changed without changing the behaviour near either state, so no quantity that characterises only the vicinity of the states can determine which is more probable. Separately, even a monostable linear circuit's steady state need not be one of minimum entropy production. Unread: filed from the abstract. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-02 from its abstract and Crossref metadata, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (Physical Review A, closed; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex list no open copy). Filed because it is the classic objection to entropy-based characterisations of nonequilibrium steady states, Prigogine's minimum principle among them; it stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-533](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-533.md) | Life as a manifestation of the second law of thermodynamics | Schneider & Kay (1994), Math. Comput. Modelling 19(6–8):25–48. A "restated second law": systems moved from equilibrium "utilize all avenues available to counter the applied gradients". Bénard convection and a vortex draining a bottle are read as structures that destroy gradients faster. Life is "another means of dissipating the solar induced gradient" (living systems as "sophisticated mini-tornados, with a memory"), and ecosystems develop to degrade more incoming exergy. A stressed marsh shows smaller flows and fewer cycles; airborne thermal scans show mature forests cooler (degrading 90% of net solar radiation against a quarry's 62%). The second law is "necessary but not sufficient" for life. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-415](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-415.md)), from the authors' own formatted text (copyright line "James J. Kay and Eric Schneider, 1992"), not the journal's typeset version. Worth reading as the canonical statement of the "gradient-dissipation" view of life: living systems and ecosystems are dissipative structures that develop so as to degrade the solar gradient more completely, and the second law is "a necessary but not sufficient cause for life". Read the thermodynamics as a programme, not a derivation. The "restated second law" is offered as a corollary of Kestin's stability result but not derived from it. The ecological evidence is one stressed-versus-control marsh pair and a few thermal-scanner and satellite comparisons, all correlational. It draws no line between living and non-living dissipative structures beyond "memory" (DNA). |
| [LIT-537](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-537.md) | Thermodynamic Theory of Structure, Stability and Fluctuations | Glansdorff & Prigogine (1971), Wiley-Interscience. The monograph of the Brussels thermodynamic stability theory. By the Nobel lecture's citations, it treats local equilibrium (ch. II), the second-order excess entropy δ²S as a Lyapounov function near equilibrium (ch. V), and the excess-entropy-production criterion far from equilibrium, including convection (ch. VII). Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scan is a lending-only copy, HathiTrust is search-only, and no publisher description or table of contents was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the monograph in which Glansdorff and Prigogine set out the thermodynamic stability theory that the Nobel lecture ([LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md)) summarizes; what it contains beyond what the lecture and Cross & Hohenberg cite from it is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-570.md) | An Organizational Account of Biological Functions | Mossio, Saborido & Moreno (2009), BJPS 60(4):813–841. A trait has a function iff it contributes to the maintenance of a self-maintaining organization, is produced and maintained under that organization's constraints, and the organization is differentiated. Closure grounds teleology and normativity in the current system, unifying etiological and dispositional accounts. Flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes have closure but no functions, because each makes a single undifferentiated contribution to its own maintenance. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-444](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-444.md)), from the HAL deposit of the submitted version. Worth reading as the organizational account of function and as the place where the organizational school says plainly that a candle flame has closure. Functions are contributions to a differentiated self-maintaining organization by traits that organization produces and maintains. Closure alone grounds teleology and norms but is shared by flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes; organizational differentiation is what functions need. Reproduction is admitted to be a problem and left to a sketch. |
| [LIT-582](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-582.md) | Biological organisation as closure of constraints | Montévil & Mossio (2015), J. Theor. Biol. 372:179–191. Two causal regimes act in organisms: processes (thermodynamic changes) and constraints, which act on processes while being conserved at the relevant time scale. Closure is mutual dependence among constraints: each is produced by a process another constraint constrains, and each helps produce another. Closure mixes slow and fast dependence, grounds functions, and is proposed as a boundary criterion. A volume-sweeping count of dependencies, the tendency to closure, separates symbionts that share an encompassing closure, and separated nested closures mark levels of organisation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-468](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-468.md)), from the authors' HAL deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the paper statement of the central claim of Biological Autonomy ([LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md)): biological organisation is closure of constraints. A constraint is defined by a symmetry: it acts on a process at a time scale at which it is itself conserved. Closure is a set of constraints each of which depends directly on another in the set and generates another, and cannot be split into two closed sets. The paper offers closure as a boundary criterion and gives a preliminary measure, the tendency to closure, for drawing boundaries between interacting organisms. It does not claim closure defines an organism. |
